title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabir's first doha. I went looking for the bad one, found no one, then searched my own heart.

A shelf sags under the weight of books, commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask. Down the lane, a weaver throws the shuttle back and forth at his loom. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf, about how much reading it takes to become wise. His count is very small.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `A WEAVER AT HIS LOOM.` → `A VERY SMALL COUNT.`

segments.voice: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua. A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one became a pandit, a truly learned one. Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters is the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page. The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. So all the learning the scholar spent his life on fits in a word you can write in a second and spend a lifetime learning to read. Kabir doesn't say books are bad; his own verses ended up in books. He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. You can read about love until you die, and never once read love itself, the way it's written in a face, in a neighbor's need, in God. And here's the trap, like yesterday's. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line asks something of them too. Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them. In Kabir's picture, love is the text, every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.
screen: `READING BOOK AFTER BOOK.` · `NOT ONE BECAME A PANDIT.` · `TWO AND A HALF LETTERS.` · then, large: `WHOEVER READS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose love you had to learn to read, someone who shows it sideways: a grandparent who fed you instead of talking, a friend who teases, a parent who worries out loud. Picture how they actually show it, and read it slowly, letter by letter, like something precious. If you pray, you can thank God for them in whatever words you already use.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: reading book after book, no one became wise; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.
Your line: two and a half letters. All that learning fits in one small word. Day nine hundred twenty-two, done.

screen: `DAY 922 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KABIR (THE DOHAS, ONE A DAY FOR A WEEK).`

howItsDone: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

chat.says: Is Kabir saying that reading holy books is a waste of time?
options: No, he says reading alone doesn't make you wise; you have to read love itself.
Yes, he says all books are bad and real seekers should never open one.
No, he says you'll be wise once you've read every sacred book there is.
chat.meaning: The doha says the world died reading and none became a pandit, but whoever reads the two and a half letters of love does.

pothi.meaning: a book, especially a sacred text

pandit.meaning: a truly learned one, a wise scholar

doha.meaning: a couplet: two rhyming lines, easy to remember

Kabir.meaning: the weaver-poet of Kashi, famous for his dohas
